syndromes.label: IGE
syndromes.name: Genetic generalized epilepsies (formerly idiopathic generalized epilepsies), overview
syndromes.ageText: Childhood to young adulthood, depending on the syndrome
syndromes.seizure: Absence, myoclonic and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, in different combinations by syndrome
syndromes.pathophys: A group of epilepsies with a strong genetic contribution and no structural cause, in which thalamo-cortical networks produce brief generalized discharges.
syndromes.eeg: Normal background with generalized, symmetric, synchronous spike-and-wave or polyspike-and-wave bursts. The rate differs by syndrome: about 3 Hz in childhood absence epilepsy, faster and with polyspikes in JME, and quicker (often 4 to 5 Hz) in eyelid myoclonia with absences. Discharges are often more frequent in drowsiness, with sleep fragmenting them.
syndromes.eegShort: Generalized spike-wave and polyspike-wave on a normal background.
syndromes.technologist: Choose activation for the likely syndrome as the request and protocol direct: hyperventilation and photic stimulation per protocol, plus sleep. Describe the discharges (rate, distribution, duration) and test responsiveness during bursts.

hyperventilation.how: Instruct deep, steady breathing at about 20 to 30 breaths per minute for 3 to 5 minutes, then keep recording for at least 1 to 3 minutes afterwards (many labs use 3; follow your lab protocol) to watch the recovery. During any burst, test responsiveness per lab protocol. Stop for a seizure or distress, and do not perform it if the request or protocol excludes it.
hyperventilation.why: It is the strongest activator for absence-type syndromes and less productive for JME.

photic.how: Standard protocol with eyes open and closed; watch for eyelid flutter. Stop at a generalized discharge or seizure sign and say so.
photic.why: Especially relevant for eyelid myoclonia with absences and photosensitive patients; less so for childhood absence.

sleepDeprivation.how: Request partial sleep deprivation per protocol and record around waking.
sleepDeprivation.why: More helpful in syndromes with jerks or convulsions on waking, such as JME.

sleep.how: Record drowsiness and sleep if allowed, with the awakening.
sleep.why: Discharges increase in drowsiness and fragment in deeper sleep.

awake.how: Record eyes open and closed.
awake.why: A routine awake record is often normal between seizures.

recording.duration: Long enough for the planned activation and, when requested, sleep.
recording.montage: Referential and bipolar views to show the generalized distribution.
recording.video: Video helps correlate absences and jerks with the bursts.
recording.ictal: During a burst, test responsiveness with a simple task or words to remember; note the length and what the patient did.
special: IGE is an umbrella term, so tailor the activation to the suspected syndrome.
Stop hyperventilation or photic stimulation for a seizure.

manifestations: Typical absence: brief staring with loss of awareness
Myoclonic jerks, usually on waking
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures
A normal neurological exam and development are typical

course.progression: Depends on the syndrome; some remit with age, others persist for life.
course.outcome: Most patients have a good outlook; the syndromes differ in how long treatment is needed.

Focal epilepsy with bilateral spread - asymmetric onset or focal spikes

Match the activation to the likely syndrome: hyperventilation for absence, photic for photosensitive syndromes, sleep deprivation and awakening for JME.
Generalized, symmetric, synchronous discharges on a normal background separate IGE from focal and symptomatic epilepsies.

Run photic stimulation per protocol and stop at the first generalized discharge or seizure.
Include drowsiness and sleep, with an awakening, when requested, and mark all events with times.

syndromes.name: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
syndromes.seizure: Rising epigastric aura, fear or deja vu, then staring, lip-smacking and hand automatisms with impaired awareness and later confusion
syndromes.pathophys: Often hippocampal sclerosis, with neuronal loss and sprouting that make the circuit hyperexcitable.
syndromes.eeg: Interictal anterior temporal sharp waves with a maximum at F7/F8 or an anterior temporal electrode, more frequent in drowsiness and sleep, often with temporal slowing. Ictal onset is rhythmic theta (about 5 to 7 Hz) that grows in amplitude, slows and spreads to adjacent regions.
syndromes.technologist: Record sleep. Use the longitudinal chain to show the phase reversal at F7/F8 (Fp1-F7 and F7-T3), and a referential montage to show that F7 or F8 has the largest amplitude. During a seizure test responsiveness and describe behaviour.
syndromes.label: Mesial TLE
syndromes.eegShort: Anterior temporal sharp waves; ictal rhythmic theta.

sleep.how: Allow drowsiness and light sleep with a natural wake-up, and record for the whole period.
sleep.why: Temporal sharp waves become more frequent in drowsiness and sleep.

sleepDeprivation.how: Request partial sleep deprivation per protocol and make sure sleep is recorded.

hyperventilation.how: Instruct deep, steady breathing at about 20 to 30 breaths per minute for 3 to 5 minutes, then keep recording for at least 1 to 3 minutes afterwards (many labs use 3; follow your lab protocol) to watch the recovery. During any burst, test responsiveness per lab protocol. Stop for a seizure or distress, and do not perform it if the request or protocol excludes it.
hyperventilation.why: It can enhance temporal slowing or spikes in some patients.

awake.how: Record eyes open and closed.
awake.why: Waking spikes may be sparse or absent, so a normal awake record does not exclude it.

recording.duration: Long enough to include sleep; a longer record or video-EEG increases the chance of capturing seizures.
recording.montage: Longitudinal and transverse bipolar chains to show phase reversal, plus referential to show the field; add anterior temporal electrodes if allowed.
recording.video: Video is essential for any extended or ictal study, to correlate the EEG with the behaviour.
recording.ictal: At the onset of an aura or seizure, press the event marker, note the clock time, test responsiveness (name, words to remember, commands), describe lip-smacking or hand movements, and keep recording through recovery with a postictal check of orientation and speech.
special: Keep the patient safe and never leave them alone.
Document what the patient reports at the aura.

manifestations: Aura: rising epigastric sensation, fear, deja vu or a smell
Behavioural arrest and staring with impaired awareness
Oral and hand automatisms, such as lip-smacking or fumbling
Contralateral dystonic posturing in some
Postictal confusion; may evolve to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure
clinical.exam: Usually normal; memory complaints are common.
clinical.imaging: MRI may show hippocampal sclerosis (mesial temporal sclerosis) or another lesion.
clinical.development: Usually normal; a history of prolonged febrile seizures is common in the mesial form.

course.onset: Most often in later childhood or the teens, with a possible seizure-free interval earlier.
course.progression: Chronic; some patients stay refractory to medication and may be evaluated for surgery.
course.outcome: Variable; patients with hippocampal sclerosis often have refractory seizures.

differential: Frontal lobe epilepsy - brief hypermotor events, often from sleep, with little postictal confusion
Occipital or parietal epilepsy - visual or sensory features and posterior spikes
Non-epileptic events - no EEG change and variable semiology
Benign temporal variants (wicket spikes, small sharp spikes) - not slowed, no aftergoing slow wave and not clustered
pearls: Anterior temporal sharp waves are maximal at F7 or F8 and more frequent in drowsiness and sleep.
Phase reversal at F7/F8 in the longitudinal chain locates the spike; the referential montage confirms the field.
Ictal onset is often rhythmic theta that builds in amplitude and slows as it spreads.
During a seizure, test responsiveness and describe automatisms with times for the reader.
Hippocampal sclerosis is the classic pathology of the mesial form.

Perform hyperventilation and photic stimulation per protocol only if requested.

syndromes.label: Juvenile absence
syndromes.name: Juvenile absence epilepsy
syndromes.seizure: Typical absences, often less frequent than in childhood absence epilepsy, with generalized tonic-clonic seizures common and occasional myoclonic jerks
syndromes.pathophys: A genetically determined generalized epilepsy in which thalamocortical networks generate generalized spike-and-wave; the network mechanism overlaps with childhood absence epilepsy.
syndromes.eeg: Normal background with generalized, bilaterally synchronous spike-and-wave bursts, often slightly faster than 3 Hz (about 3.5 to 4.5 Hz) and sometimes with polyspikes. Bursts may last a few seconds to over 10 seconds.
syndromes.eegShort: Generalized spike-and-wave a little faster than 3 Hz on a normal background.
syndromes.technologist: Test responsiveness during bursts and note the time and what was said. Perform hyperventilation, and record both awake and drowsy or sleep states.

hyperventilation.how: Do 3 to 5 minutes of deep breathing with good effort and keep recording afterwards. Stop for a prolonged seizure, distress, or if the patient cannot cooperate.
hyperventilation.why: It often provokes bursts, though less reliably than in childhood absence.

sleepDeprivation.how: Follow the lab's sleep-restriction instructions and record through the transition to sleep and the awakening.
sleepDeprivation.why: Sleep loss often increases discharges and the chance of capturing an event.

sleep.how: Record drowsiness, sleep and the period after awakening.
sleep.why: Discharges may increase, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures are more likely near awakening.

photic.how: Run the lab's standard intermittent photic protocol, each frequency with eyes open then eyes closed, and stop at once on a photoparoxysmal response or seizure.
photic.why: It occasionally brings out discharges and is part of the full protocol.

awake.how: Include eyes-open and eyes-closed periods.
awake.why: Bursts may appear without provocation.

recording.duration: An awake record with hyperventilation and photic stimulation, plus drowsiness or sleep if possible; at least 20 to 30 minutes awake.
recording.montage: Referential and bipolar views to show the generalized distribution.
recording.video: Use video when available to document staring, brief lapses and any myoclonic jerks.
recording.ictal: During a burst, test responsiveness, mark the time and record what was said; note a tonic-clonic seizure with time and sequence if one occurs.
special: Stop hyperventilation or photic stimulation if a seizure begins and stay with the patient.
Record the medication list and last dose time.

manifestations: Impaired awareness with staring, usually without marked automatisms
Absences are less frequent than in childhood absence epilepsy and can last longer
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are common, often near waking
Myoclonic jerks may occur
clinical.development: Usually normal.

course.onset: From about 8 years through the teens; peak around puberty.
course.progression: Absences tend to persist, and tonic-clonic seizures may continue into adulthood.
course.outcome: Often remains lifelong or needs long-term follow-up; less likely to remit than childhood absence epilepsy.

differential: Childhood absence epilepsy - younger onset, more frequent absences, regular 3 Hz
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy - myoclonic jerks on waking, polyspike-wave
Jeavons syndrome - eyelid myoclonia with eye closure sensitivity
Focal seizures with impaired awareness - different EEG and onset
pearls: The spike-and-wave is often a little faster than the 3 Hz of childhood absence.
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are more common than in childhood absence epilepsy.
Hyperventilation and sleep-deprived studies are the usual activation tools.
syndromes.sceneNote: The tracing shows a generalized spike-and-wave burst at about 3.6 to 4 Hz lasting about 5.6 seconds in an awake 14-year-old.
yieldPlan: Record the medication list and last dose time, and ask about recent sleep and whether seizures occur on waking.
Begin with an awake baseline, then do hyperventilation for 3 to 5 minutes and continue recording afterwards.
Add standard photic stimulation, noting any photoparoxysmal response and stopping at once if one appears.
Test responsiveness during every burst and mark the time and what the patient said or did.
Arrange drowsiness and sleep, ideally following the lab's sleep-restriction instruction, and keep recording through awakening.

syndromes.name: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
syndromes.seizure: Myoclonic jerks, especially soon after waking; generalized tonic-clonic seizures; absences in some
syndromes.pathophys: A genetic generalized epilepsy with a hyperexcitable frontal-thalamic network. Sleep deprivation, alcohol and flashing lights lower the threshold.
syndromes.eeg: Normal background with brief generalized polyspike-and-slow-wave complexes (a burst of 4 to 6 Hz polyspike-wave may repeat for 1 to 3 seconds), often frontal predominant, sometimes with a photoparoxysmal response. Bursts are often activated by sleep deprivation and by awakening.
syndromes.technologist: Record on waking or after sleep deprivation if requested. Mark jerks with the time. Photic stimulation per protocol, stopping at the first sign of a photoparoxysmal discharge.
syndromes.label: JME
syndromes.eegShort: Generalized 4 to 6 Hz polyspike-wave bursts, often frontal predominant.

sleepDeprivation.how: Arrange partial sleep deprivation as the protocol or requester states (the amount is set by the lab; follow the instructions given to the family) and record soon after waking. Confirm and note the actual sleep hours; do not give stimulants.
sleepDeprivation.why: Discharges and jerks cluster around waking, so a sleep-deprived record with an awakening is the most likely to capture them.

sleep.how: Let the patient drowse and sleep, then wake them and continue recording for several minutes. Mark the time of waking.
sleep.why: Discharges are activated by drowsiness and the awakening itself.

photic.how: Run the standard intermittent photic protocol, including the 15 to 20 Hz range, with eyes open and then closed. Watch the patient as well as the tracing. Stop the flashes immediately at a generalized discharge, a jerk or any seizure sign, and say so in the report.
photic.why: A photoparoxysmal response occurs in a sizeable minority, and flashes can trigger a jerk or convulsion.

hyperventilation.how: Instruct deep, steady breathing at about 20 to 30 breaths per minute for 3 to 5 minutes, then keep recording for at least 1 to 3 minutes afterwards (many labs use 3; follow your lab protocol) to watch the recovery. During any burst, test responsiveness per lab protocol. Stop for a seizure or distress, and do not perform it if the request or protocol excludes it.
hyperventilation.why: Less productive here than sleep deprivation, but still performed per protocol.

awake.how: Record eyes open and closed; add simple hand tasks only if the protocol permits and the patient can do them safely.
awake.why: A short awake-only record is often normal.

recording.duration: Allow enough time to include drowsiness, sleep and a documented awakening; a short awake-only study may be normal.
recording.montage: Run both referential and bipolar montages so the generalized, symmetric distribution and frontal emphasis are shown.
recording.video: Use video if available, with an EMG channel on the deltoid or forearm extensors to time jerks against the polyspike bursts.
recording.ictal: If a jerk series or convulsion occurs, mark the time, keep the patient safe, describe what was seen and test responsiveness during the burst; keep recording through the aftermath.
special: Record on waking: this is when jerks and discharges are most likely.
Stop photic stimulation at the first sign of a photoparoxysmal discharge or seizure.
Note the medication list and last dose time.

manifestations: Brief, bilateral, symmetric jerks of the shoulders and arms, most often shortly after waking; objects may be dropped
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures, often after waking or after sleep loss
Absence seizures in a minority
Consciousness is usually preserved during the jerks
clinical.development: Normal intelligence and development in most patients.

course.onset: Usually in the teenage years, with jerks often appearing before the first convulsion.
course.progression: A lifelong tendency; the tendency is lifelong.
course.outcome: Seizures are controlled in most patients with treatment, but a long-term course is typical.

differential: Childhood and juvenile absence epilepsy - absence is the main seizure type and there are no myoclonic jerks
Epilepsy with generalized tonic-clonic seizures alone - no jerks or absences
Progressive myoclonus epilepsies - abnormal exam, slowed background and a progressive course
Frontal lobe seizures - focal onset and asymmetric features rather than symmetric generalized bursts
pearls: The EEG finding to look for is generalized polyspike-and-wave, usually faster than the 3 Hz spike-and-wave of childhood absence epilepsy.
Jerks cluster after waking, so recording after sleep or at awakening is the key activation.
Mark the exact time of any jerk so the reader can match it to the polyspike burst.
Photic stimulation can provoke discharges and convulsions; stop at the first discharge.
The background is normal between bursts, which separates JME from symptomatic generalized epilepsy.
yieldPlan: Check the request and record the medication list, last dose time, hours slept and time of the last jerk.
Schedule the study soon after the patient wakes, ideally after partial sleep deprivation (often about 4 to 6 hours of sleep, or as your protocol states).
Record awake first with eyes open and closed, then hyperventilation for 3 to 5 minutes per protocol.
Run photic stimulation per protocol, covering the 15 to 20 Hz range, and stop at the first generalized discharge or jerk.
Allow the patient to drowse or sleep, then wake them and keep recording through the awakening, asking them to hold out their arms or do a simple task.
Mark every jerk with clock time, which limb moved and whether the patient was aware; test responsiveness during any burst.

syndromes.label: GTCA
syndromes.name: Epilepsy with generalized tonic-clonic seizures alone (GTCA)
syndromes.ageText: Peak in adolescence; onset from about 5 to 40 years
syndromes.seizure: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are the only seizure type, often shortly after waking or from sleep
syndromes.pathophys: A genetic generalized epilepsy in which cortico-thalamic networks are hyperexcitable. Sleep loss, alcohol and fatigue lower the threshold.
syndromes.eeg: Normal background with brief generalized spike-and-wave or polyspike-and-wave bursts, typically 3 to 6 Hz, symmetric and synchronous. Discharges are often more frequent in drowsiness and after waking. During a convulsion, the tonic phase brings generalized fast activity, followed by rhythmic bursts and then postictal slowing.
syndromes.eegShort: Generalized 3 to 6 Hz spike-wave and polyspike-wave on a normal background.
syndromes.technologist: Record drowsiness, sleep and an awakening if the protocol allows. Perform activation per protocol and mark any clinical event with its time. If a convulsion occurs, keep the patient safe, describe the onset and the behaviour, and keep recording through the postictal period.

sleepDeprivation.how: Arrange partial sleep deprivation as the protocol states and record soon after waking. Confirm and note the sleep hours.
sleepDeprivation.why: Seizures and discharges cluster after waking, so this raises the chance of capturing them.

sleep.how: Include drowsiness, sleep and a documented awakening, and keep recording for several minutes after waking.
sleep.why: Discharges and seizures cluster in drowsiness and around waking.

hyperventilation.how: Instruct deep, steady breathing at about 20 to 30 breaths per minute for 3 to 5 minutes, then keep recording for at least 1 to 3 minutes afterwards (many labs use 3; follow your lab protocol) to watch the recovery. During any burst, test responsiveness per lab protocol. Stop for a seizure or distress, and do not perform it if the request or protocol excludes it.
hyperventilation.why: It may bring out generalized discharges.

photic.how: Run the standard protocol with eyes open and closed and stop at the first generalized discharge or seizure sign.
photic.why: A photoparoxysmal response is less typical than in JME but is possible.

awake.how: Record eyes open and closed with a calm patient.
awake.why: An awake record may be normal or show only occasional bursts.

recording.duration: Long enough to include sleep and an awakening; a short awake record can be normal.
recording.montage: Use referential and bipolar views to show the generalized, symmetric distribution.
recording.video: Use video if available so a convulsion can be matched to the EEG.
recording.ictal: In a convulsion, mark onset, keep the patient safe without restraining, describe the tonic and clonic phases with times, and keep recording through the postictal period.
special: Seizures often follow waking, so keep the patient observed during the awakening.
Never leave the patient alone after sleep deprivation or a seizure.

manifestations: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure with loss of awareness, stiffening, then rhythmic jerking
Seizures often occur soon after waking or during sleep
By definition no absence seizures or myoclonic jerks (a careful history is needed to be sure)
clinical.development: Normal.

course.onset: Mostly in the second decade, with a wide range.
course.progression: Variable; some patients stay free of seizures, in others the tendency persists.
course.outcome: Seizures are controlled in many patients; some patients later reveal myoclonic or absence seizures, which changes the syndrome label.

differential: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy - the history includes myoclonic jerks, and polyspike-wave is usually present
Childhood or juvenile absence epilepsy - absence seizures are a defining feature
Focal epilepsy with secondary generalization - focal onset or focal spikes, and asymmetry
Convulsive syncope or non-epileptic events - no epileptiform change on EEG
pearls: GTCA means convulsions only: no absences and no myoclonic jerks.
Seizures cluster around awakening, so recording drowsiness and the awakening adds value.
The interictal EEG may be normal; a normal record does not exclude the syndrome.
During a convulsion, muscle artifact hides the cortical rhythm, so the clinical description and timing carry the information.
The normal background and normal exam and imaging separate it from symptomatic generalized epilepsy.
syndromes.sceneNote: Awake 17-year-old with a generalized 4 to 4.6 Hz spike-wave burst and a polyspike-wave complex on a normal background.
yieldPlan: Record the medication list, last dose time, sleep hours and the time of the last convulsion.
Arrange the study after partial sleep deprivation, soon after waking, if requested.
Start with an awake record, eyes open and closed, then hyperventilation and photic stimulation per protocol.
Let the patient drowse and sleep, then wake them and keep recording through the awakening.
Be ready for a convulsion: protect the patient, mark the onset time and keep recording through the postictal period.
Describe the discharges (rate, distribution, duration) and mark any event with its clock time.

patterns.name: Lateralized periodic discharges (LPDs, formerly PLEDs) in a focal destructive illness
patterns.context: For example acute herpes simplex encephalitis involving one temporal lobe
patterns.eeg: Periodic sharp or sharp-and-slow complexes about every 1 to 2 seconds, lateralized to the affected temporal region, over focal delta and slowing.
patterns.pathophys: Acute necrosis of cortex and deafferentation produce stereotyped repeating discharges.
patterns.technologist: Describe the interval between complexes and the side, record state and medications, and tell the reader promptly if the pattern changes.

patterns.name: Generalized periodic discharges (GPDs) in a rapidly progressive dementia
patterns.eeg: Stereotyped bi- or triphasic sharp complexes repeating about once per second, generalized and usually fairly symmetric (they can be asymmetric early), on a slowed background. They may disappear in very advanced disease.
patterns.pathophys: Widespread cortical neuronal loss and spongiform change, with synchronous bursts of activity.
patterns.technologist: Record stimulus responses (the complexes may be reduced by sedation). Describe the rate and distribution. Follow the facility prion policy: use disposable electrodes and supplies and do not reuse cup or needle electrodes.

patterns.name: Periodic complexes in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis
patterns.context: A late complication of measles in a child or adolescent, with myoclonic jerks
patterns.eeg: Stereotyped high-amplitude generalized complexes recurring every 4 to 10 seconds, often time-locked to a myoclonic jerk, on a slowed background.
patterns.pathophys: Persistent viral infection of the brain that damages cortex and white matter.
patterns.technologist: Use a long page (or time base) so the long interval is visible, and mark each jerk with the time.

patterns.name: Alpha coma
patterns.context: A comatose patient after cardiac arrest or with a brainstem lesion
patterns.eeg: Generalized alpha-range activity (8 to 12 Hz) that is frontally predominant and does not react to stimulation. The pattern is unlike a normal posterior alpha rhythm, which blocks with eye opening.
patterns.pathophys: A pathological rhythm produced by injured cortex and its brainstem or thalamic connections, which no longer respond to input.
patterns.technologist: Test and record reactivity with every protocol stimulus. Describe the distribution and frequency, and the medications and temperature if known.

patterns.name: Drug-induced beta activity
patterns.context: A patient taking a benzodiazepine or barbiturate
patterns.eeg: Excess beta (about 13 to 30 Hz), generalized and frontally predominant, often in an otherwise normal record. The posterior rhythm may be present or reduced.
patterns.pathophys: Enhanced GABA-A receptor activity changes the thalamocortical rhythms.
patterns.technologist: Record the medications and doses with their times. Describe the activity without naming the cause.

mistakes: The scalp EEG records action potentials.
It records summed postsynaptic potentials from synchronously active pyramidal neurons.
A small cortical focus will always show on the scalp.
A small area, or a focus deep in a sulcus or on the medial surface, can be invisible; several square centimetres of synchronous cortex are needed.
Delta waves always mean damage.
Delta is normal in deep sleep. Focal polymorphic delta while awake points to a focal lesion (often white matter) that has deafferented the cortex; the reader judges the cause.
A normal interictal EEG rules out epilepsy.
A single routine EEG shows epileptiform discharges in only about half of patients with epilepsy or fewer, and less often in frontal lobe epilepsy. Repeat studies and sleep raise the yield.
Absence seizures come from a single cortical focus.
They arise in an abnormal thalamocortical loop and produce generalized, symmetric discharges.
Hypsarrhythmia means the cause is known.
It is a pattern, not a diagnosis. Many causes produce it.
Rolandic spikes are always on one side.
They can shift sides and can be bilateral; sleep activates them.
Temporal lobe seizures start with generalized convulsions.
They typically start with an aura and automatisms; a generalized convulsion is a later spread.
The alpha rhythm in a comatose patient is a good sign.
Alpha that is frontally dominant and unreactive in coma (alpha coma) is a pathological pattern.
The technologist can name the syndrome from the EEG.
The reader interprets and diagnoses. The technologist describes with numbers, marks events and documents state and medications.

genetics.intro: Genes do not give an EEG pattern by themselves. Many genes cause the same pattern, and one gene can cause different patterns at different ages. Use this tab to link the age, the EEG and the associated signs to the conditions the reader may consider. A technologist records and describes; the reader and the clinician make the genetic diagnosis.
principles: One pattern, many genes: hypsarrhythmia and burst suppression have many genetic and non-genetic causes.
One gene, many patterns: the EEG changes with age, so the same gene can show burst suppression in a neonate and hypsarrhythmia later.
A normal EEG does not exclude a genetic disorder, especially for NF1, NF2 and the first study in SCN1A or CDKL5.
Skin, head size, behavior and movements are part of your report: describe them, and note how artifact from hand stereotypies, laughing or muscle appears.
patternTable: Nonspecific; other encephalopathies can look similar
Nonspecific: also seen with subdural fluid, infarct or scalp swelling; compare sides at equal sensitivity
Drugs also cause beta; check the history
The interictal EEG is often normal

items.label: Tuberous sclerosis
items.name: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC)
items.age: Seizures usually begin in the first year; infantile spasms are common
items.clinical: Autosomal dominant, and most cases are new (de novo) variants. Features: cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, hypomelanotic skin patches, facial angiofibromas, cardiac and kidney tumours. Most patients have epilepsy, often starting as infantile spasms or focal seizures.
items.mechanism: The TSC1/TSC2 protein complex normally restrains the mTOR growth pathway. Loss of function over-activates mTOR, which produces tubers and hyperexcitable cortex.
items.eeg: Infantile spasms: hypsarrhythmia, often asymmetric or with a clear focal emphasis, and an electrodecrement at each spasm. Later: focal or multifocal spikes, often over tubers, with focal slowing. Tubers can be in any lobe, so the spike field can be anywhere.
items.technologist: Mark every spasm with its time and record both hemispheres at the same sensitivity so asymmetry is visible. Describe where the spikes are largest in referential and bipolar montages. The reader links the findings to imaging.
items.sceneNote: Classic symmetric hypsarrhythmia is shown (in TSC it is often asymmetric); later in childhood, a focal spike field over a right posterior temporal tuber.
yieldPlan: Record the medication list and last dose time, and ask the caregiver to describe the usual events (spasms, focal seizures).
Record an awake and, if possible, a sleep segment, because spikes and hypsarrhythmia are most apparent in non-REM sleep.
Keep the same sensitivity on both hemispheres so asymmetry and a focal emphasis are visible; run referential and bipolar views.
Use video and a deltoid or neck EMG channel when spasms are suspected so each spasm can be matched to the electrodecrement.
Mark every spasm and seizure with clock time, and describe the movements, cluster pattern and responsiveness.
Add photic stimulation and hyperventilation only if age and cooperation allow, per protocol.

sleep.how: Allow natural sleep and record both light and deep non-REM, plus the awakening, which is when spasms cluster.
sleep.why: Hypsarrhythmia, focal spikes and electrodecrement are most evident in sleep.

awake.how: Record a calm awake segment, eyes open and closed; note tone and alertness.
awake.why: Shows the background and any focal slowing over tubers.

photic.how: Per lab protocol, with the room dim and eyes open, then closed; stop at once for a photoparoxysmal response or clinical event and mark the frequency.
photic.why: Not a main activator in TSC, but part of a complete study.

hyperventilation.how: Only if the child is old enough to cooperate (blowing a pinwheel or tissue works). Never force it. Stop for distress or any event.
hyperventilation.why: Rarely adds yield in infants and may be impossible.

recording.duration: Long enough to include sleep and at least one awakening; follow the lab protocol, extending if events are expected.
recording.montage: Full age-appropriate montage covering all lobes, since tubers can be anywhere; add EMG for spasms.
recording.video: Video synchronized to EEG, with the camera framing the whole body and face.
recording.ictal: Press the event marker at the first sign of a spasm or seizure, note the clock time, describe the movements, test responsiveness when safe, and record what happens afterwards.
special: Spasms often occur in clusters on waking.
Report the spike location in both referential and bipolar views; the reader links it to imaging.

items.label: Neurofibromatosis 1
items.name: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
items.age: Clinical features appear in childhood; seizures are uncommon
items.clinical: Autosomal dominant (about half are new variants). Features: cafe-au-lait spots, skin-fold freckling, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, learning problems. Epilepsy occurs in a minority, much less often than in TSC.
items.mechanism: Neurofibromin is a negative regulator of the RAS pathway; loss of function over-activates RAS and mTOR signalling.
items.eeg: Often normal or nonspecific. Focal slowing or focal spikes appear only when there is a cortical lesion or tumour. There is no characteristic NF1 pattern.
items.technologist: Record a standard study and describe any focal finding. Do not expect a distinctive pattern; a normal EEG does not exclude the disorder.
yieldPlan: Record the medication list and last dose time, and note the clinical reason (spells, tumour, cognition).
Record a standard awake study including drowsiness and, if the patient falls asleep, a sleep segment, since sleep gives the best chance of capturing focal discharges.
Include hyperventilation and photic stimulation per protocol, and mark any focal change.
Describe any focal slowing or spikes and their location; check electrode placement over any scalp neurofibroma or skin lesion.
Mark and describe any clinical event with time. A normal record does not exclude the disorder.

awake.how: Record a full awake segment with eyes open and closed.
awake.why: The main yield is documenting a focal abnormality if a lesion is present.

sleep.how: Let the patient drowse or sleep if they can, and record the stages.
sleep.why: Sleep increases the chance of capturing focal epileptiform activity.

hyperventilation.how: Per lab protocol, about 3 minutes of hyperventilation with good effort, then 2 to 3 minutes after. Watch the patient throughout, mark the start, end and effort quality, and stop for a seizure or distress.
hyperventilation.why: Standard activation; does not target NF1.

photic.how: Per lab protocol, with the room dim and eyes open, then closed; stop at once for a photoparoxysmal response or clinical event and mark the frequency.
photic.why: Standard activation; does not target NF1.

recording.duration: Standard length per protocol, extending only if the clinician requests sleep.
recording.montage: Standard age-appropriate montage; add extra electrodes over a known lesion if ordered.
recording.video: Use video only if spells are being investigated.
recording.ictal: Mark and describe any event with time and responsiveness testing.
special: There is no characteristic NF1 EEG pattern; a normal EEG does not exclude the disorder.
Take care over scalp neurofibromas.

items.label: Neurofibromatosis 2
items.name: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
items.age: Usually teen years to young adulthood
items.clinical: Autosomal dominant. Features: bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, spinal tumours. Seizures are uncommon and are usually due to a meningioma or other tumour.
items.mechanism: Merlin is a tumour suppressor; its loss causes schwannomas and meningiomas rather than a primary cortical excitability disorder.
items.eeg: Often normal. Focal slowing or spikes can occur near a meningioma.
items.technologist: Hearing loss is common and can be profound, so test responsiveness with touch and visual stimuli as well as voice. Record and describe any focal finding.
yieldPlan: Record the medication list and last dose time, and note the clinical reason.
Check hearing: hearing loss can be profound, so give instructions in writing or by gesture and test responsiveness with touch and visual stimuli as well as voice.
Record a standard awake and drowsy study, with sleep if it occurs, per protocol.
Include hyperventilation and photic stimulation per protocol, and describe any focal finding and its location.
Mark any event with time. A normal record does not exclude the disorder.

awake.how: Record eyes open and closed with clear non-verbal instructions.
awake.why: Shows any focal slowing near a meningioma.

sleep.how: Allow drowsiness and sleep if they occur.
sleep.why: Increases the chance of capturing focal spikes.

hyperventilation.how: Per lab protocol, about 3 minutes of hyperventilation with good effort, then 2 to 3 minutes after. Watch the patient throughout, mark the start, end and effort quality, and stop for a seizure or distress. Give instructions by demonstration if hearing is poor.
hyperventilation.why: Standard activation.

photic.how: Per lab protocol, with the room dim and eyes open, then closed; stop at once for a photoparoxysmal response or clinical event and mark the frequency.
photic.why: Standard activation.

recording.duration: Standard length per protocol.
recording.montage: Standard age-appropriate montage; add electrodes over a known lesion if ordered.
recording.video: Video only if events are being investigated.
recording.ictal: Mark and describe events with time and a visual or touch responsiveness check.
special: Hearing loss may make verbal responsiveness testing unreliable.
A normal EEG does not exclude the disorder.

items.label: Sturge-Weber
items.name: Sturge-Weber syndrome
items.gene: GNAQ, a somatic (mosaic) variant, not inherited
items.age: Seizures usually begin in the first year
items.clinical: Port-wine stain on the face (often the forehead and upper eyelid), a leptomeningeal angioma and glaucoma on the same side as the stain, and later weakness (hemiparesis) on the opposite side of the body. Seizures are common and may be focal, with clusters or prolonged episodes.
items.mechanism: A somatic GNAQ variant in some cells causes abnormal vessels. Chronic poor venous drainage and low blood flow damage the underlying cortex.
items.eeg: Reduced amplitude and fast activity over the affected hemisphere compared with the other side (attenuation), with focal or multifocal spikes and slowing there.
items.technologist: Use the same sensitivity on both sides and compare them. Place electrodes with care over a port-wine stain or scalp lesion, and note any skin changes. Describe the amplitude asymmetry rather than naming the side as abnormal.
items.sceneNote: Right hemisphere attenuation with a right posterior spike.
yieldPlan: Record the medication list and last dose time, and note the side of the port-wine stain.
Place electrodes with care over a port-wine stain or lesion, and do not abrade the skin there; document any deviation from the standard placement.
Use identical sensitivity on both hemispheres and keep symmetric electrode contact so amplitude asymmetry is real.
Record awake and sleep, and compare the two hemispheres in both states.
Mark every seizure with time; describe where the movement began and whether it was lateralized.
Document the amplitude asymmetry as an observation and leave interpretation to the reader.

awake.how: Record a full awake segment, eyes open and closed, with the same sensitivity on both sides.
awake.why: Shows reduced amplitude and fast activity over the affected side.

sleep.how: Record drowsiness and sleep with spindle and slow-wave symmetry noted.
sleep.why: Spikes and focal slowing are more evident in sleep.

photic.how: Per lab protocol, with the room dim and eyes open, then closed; stop at once for a photoparoxysmal response or clinical event and mark the frequency.
photic.why: Part of a complete study.

hyperventilation.how: Only if the child is old enough to cooperate (blowing a pinwheel or tissue works). Never force it. Stop for distress or any event.
hyperventilation.why: Rarely adds yield and may be impossible in young children.

recording.duration: Long enough for awake and sleep, per protocol.
recording.montage: Symmetric full montage; confirm electrode contact over skin lesions with impedance checks.
recording.video: Use video when seizures are expected or reported.
recording.ictal: Mark each event with time, describe laterality, test responsiveness when safe, and note afterwards.
special: Port-wine stain skin may be fragile or vascular; avoid abrasion and follow lab protocol.
Describe the asymmetry rather than naming a side as abnormal.

items.label: SCN1A / Dravet
items.name: SCN1A epilepsies (Dravet syndrome and GEFS+)
items.age: Dravet: first seizure around 6 months, often with fever
items.clinical: Fever-sensitive, often prolonged seizures in a previously normal infant, then multiple seizure types and developmental slowing. A milder variant is genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+).
items.mechanism: Loss of function of the sodium channel in inhibitory interneurons reduces inhibition, so the network becomes hyperexcitable.
items.eeg: The first EEG can be normal. Later: generalized and multifocal spike-wave, photosensitivity, and background slowing. See the Dravet card on the Syndromes tab.
items.technologist: Record sleep and photic stimulation per protocol and stop for a clinical event. Note temperature or illness, and the timing of any seizure.
yieldPlan: Record the medication list and last dose time, and ask about temperature, recent illness and warm environments.
Keep the room at a comfortable temperature and monitor the patient: heat and fever can provoke seizures.
Include photic stimulation per protocol, with the room dim, because photosensitivity is common; stop at once for a photoparoxysmal response or seizure.
Record sleep, since discharges become more frequent and multifocal in drowsiness and sleep.
Use video with the whole body in frame and mark each event with time.
A normal first EEG is possible; document that the record does not exclude the disorder.

photic.how: Per lab protocol with the room dim, eyes open then closed; stop at once for a photoparoxysmal response or seizure, and mark the frequency.
photic.why: Photosensitivity is common in Dravet.

sleep.how: Record drowsiness and sleep, and note the stages.
sleep.why: Discharges often increase in sleep.

hyperventilation.how: Only if the child is old enough to cooperate (blowing a pinwheel or tissue works). Never force it. Stop for distress or any event.
hyperventilation.why: Often impossible in young children; use only if the patient can cooperate.

awake.how: Record eyes open and closed for background assessment.
awake.why: Shows slowing as the disorder progresses.

recording.duration: Long enough for awake and sleep, plus any event; follow the lab protocol.
recording.montage: Age-appropriate full montage with ECG; add EMG for myoclonus if ordered.
recording.video: Video EEG is valuable for myoclonic and focal seizures.
recording.ictal: Mark onset with the event button, note the clock time, observe the movements, test responsiveness when safe, and record temperature or illness.
special: Prolonged or febrile seizures can occur; know the lab emergency plan and call for help early.
Do not infer the gene from the pattern.

items.label: SCN2A / SCN8A
items.name: SCN2A and SCN8A developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
items.age: Early-onset forms start in the neonatal or early infant period
items.clinical: Early seizures, often focal or tonic, with developmental delay. SCN2A also has a later-onset form with autism and intellectual disability. Variants that increase channel function tend to cause the early forms.
items.mechanism: Gain-of-function variants make excitatory neurons fire too easily; some SCN2A variants reduce function instead and give a later, different phenotype.
items.eeg: Variable: multifocal spikes, focal discharges, burst suppression or hypsarrhythmia in early infancy, depending on the stage.
items.technologist: Record states and any events with time markers, and describe the distribution of discharges. Do not infer a gene from the pattern.
yieldPlan: Record the medication list and last dose time, and ask about events seen at home.
Use the age-appropriate neonatal or infant montage and include ECG, with respiration and EMG polygraphic channels if the lab uses them.
Record both awake and sleep states and label them: discharges and background differ in each.
Keep video on throughout and mark every event with time, because some movements are not seizures.
Describe the distribution of discharges (focal, multifocal, burst suppression or hypsarrhythmia) in each state.
Do not infer a gene from the pattern.

sleep.how: Record active and quiet sleep or non-REM sleep and the awakening, with states labelled.
sleep.why: Discharges and burst patterns are state-dependent.

awake.how: Record a calm awake segment with eyes open when possible.
awake.why: Shows the awake background and any ictal events.

photic.how: Per lab protocol, with the room dim and eyes open, then closed; stop at once for a photoparoxysmal response or clinical event and mark the frequency. Only in older infants who can be tested.
photic.why: Part of a complete study when age allows.

hyperventilation.how: Do not attempt in neonates or infants.
hyperventilation.why: Not feasible at this age.

recording.duration: Long enough to capture sleep states and events; neonatal studies are often longer. Follow the lab protocol.
recording.montage: Use the age-appropriate neonatal or infant montage and electrode set per lab protocol, with electrode impedance checked and an ECG channel; add respiration and EMG polygraphic channels if the lab uses them. Do not invent parameters beyond the lab protocol.
recording.video: Continuous synchronized video with the whole infant in frame.
recording.ictal: Mark each event with the event button and clock time, describe movements, and record whether the EEG changed.
special: Neonatal movements and tremors can mimic seizures.
Do not infer the gene from the EEG pattern.

items.label: KCNQ2
items.name: KCNQ2 neonatal epilepsies
items.age: Neonate, usually in the first week
items.clinical: Mild form: self-limited familial neonatal seizures with a normal outcome. Severe form: neonatal epileptic encephalopathy with tonic seizures and developmental delay.
items.mechanism: Loss of potassium channel function (the M-current) lets neurons depolarize and fire too easily.
items.eeg: Self-limited form: interictal EEG is often normal or nonspecific. The severe form can show burst suppression or multifocal discharges, and an ictal attenuation can start a seizure.
items.technologist: Record in a neonate with the correct neonatal montage and mark each clinical event with time. Describe the seizure semiology you saw.
items.sceneNote: Burst suppression is nonspecific; the severe form can resemble it, but its seizures often start with an ictal attenuation.
yieldPlan: Record the medication list and last dose time, and note gestational age and age in days.
Apply the correct neonatal montage and keep the baby calm, warm and supervised.
Record sleep states and label them; in the severe form note burst suppression or multifocal discharges.
Use video on throughout with the face and limbs in frame.
Mark every clinical event with clock time, and describe the semiology (tonic, autonomic, focal clonic) and responsiveness.
The interictal EEG may be normal; this does not exclude the disorder.

sleep.how: Record active sleep, quiet sleep and wake cycles, with states labelled.
sleep.why: State changes may reveal the background and discharges.

awake.how: Record when the infant is awake and calm.
awake.why: Shows the background and any events.

photic.how: Do not use photic stimulation in a neonate unless ordered.
photic.why: Not a standard neonatal activation.

hyperventilation.how: Do not attempt in neonates.
hyperventilation.why: Not feasible.

recording.duration: Long enough to capture sleep states and ideally events; neonatal studies are often long. Follow the lab protocol.
recording.montage: Use the age-appropriate neonatal or infant montage and electrode set per lab protocol, with electrode impedance checked and an ECG channel; add respiration and EMG polygraphic channels if the lab uses them. Do not invent parameters beyond the lab protocol.
recording.video: Continuous video synchronized to EEG.
recording.ictal: Use the event marker at the first sign of an event, note the clock time and describe the semiology and any autonomic change.
special: Handle gently and keep warm.
A normal interictal EEG does not exclude the disorder.

items.label: CDKL5
items.name: CDKL5 deficiency disorder
items.age: Seizures usually start in the first 3 months
items.clinical: Early, hard-to-treat seizures (often tonic) in a baby, then epileptic spasms in many, severe developmental delay and poor eye contact. Females are more often diagnosed.
items.mechanism: Loss of a kinase that is important for neuronal maturation and synapse function.
items.eeg: The EEG may be normal for the first weeks, then show multifocal discharges and slowing. Hypsarrhythmia can appear when spasms start.
items.technologist: Mark spasms and tonic seizures with times. Several short studies may be needed because the first record can be normal.
yieldPlan: Record the medication list and last dose time, and ask the caregiver to describe spasms and tonic seizures.
Use the age-appropriate infant montage, with ECG and an EMG channel (deltoid or neck) per lab protocol if spasms are suspected.
Include an awake segment and a sleep segment, including the awakening.
Keep video on throughout and mark each spasm and tonic seizure with clock time.
Describe the background and discharges in each state; the first record may be normal.
If the first record is normal, note this and tell the clinician that a repeat study may be needed.

sleep.how: Record drowsiness, sleep and the awakening.
sleep.why: Multifocal discharges and hypsarrhythmia are more evident in sleep.

awake.how: Record when calm, eyes open.
awake.why: Shows the background.

recordingGuide.intro: A routine EEG is a standardized recording plus a set of activation procedures (eye opening and closure, hyperventilation, photic stimulation, sleep) that bring out abnormalities not visible in the resting waking record. The technologist's job is to record cleanly, observe the patient, test and document responsiveness, and mark everything precisely; interpretation and diagnosis belong to the physician, and exact parameters follow your lab protocol.

procedures.title: Set-up, electrodes and montages
steps: Identify the patient, record medications, last meal, sleep history, seizure history and any head injury or skull defect before applying electrodes.
Measure the head and place electrodes by the International 10-20 system (add 10-10 or supplementary electrodes when your protocol or the clinical question requires it).
Prepare the skin and keep electrode impedances within your lab's limit (between 100 ohms and 5 kilohms, per your lab protocol, with matched values between electrodes).
Add an ECG channel and eye-movement and, as needed, EMG or respiration channels to help identify artifact and state.
Run the calibration and biological-calibration (eye blink, eye movement, jaw clench) checks and confirm filter and sensitivity settings per lab protocol.
Display the record in standard bipolar (longitudinal and transverse) and referential montages, and switch montages as needed to localize and verify findings.
stop: Stop and fix the problem if electrode impedance, a floating electrode or persistent artifact makes the record uninterpretable.
Call the physician or supervisor if you find skin breakdown, a scalp wound or an unexpected skull defect that changes electrode placement.
document: Record patient identifiers, date and time, age, medications, state of alertness, last sleep and meal, and reason for the study.
Note any electrodes added, omitted or moved, and the montages, filters and sensitivities used.
procedures.tip: A clean, well-labeled technical set-up prevents most artifact that can be mistaken for epileptiform activity or hide it.

procedures.title: Recording length and state
steps: Record a minimum of about 20 to 30 minutes of technically adequate EEG (per your lab protocol), not counting set-up or time lost to artifact.
Include wakefulness with eyes open and closed, and capture drowsiness and sleep whenever the patient can achieve it.
Keep the patient comfortable, supported and relaxed so that muscle and movement artifact stays low.
Observe the patient continuously, noting state changes (alert, drowsy, asleep) as they occur.
Extend the recording when the study is borderline, when the patient fails to fall asleep and sleep is needed, or when events are expected, according to your protocol or physician request.
stop: Call the physician or supervisor if the patient cannot cooperate, is medically unstable, or an event occurs that needs care.
End or pause the study when the patient is unsafe or cannot continue, and document the reason.
document: Record start and stop time, the sequence of activations performed, and any activation omitted with the reason.
Mark state changes and note total technically adequate recording time.
procedures.tip: Time spent getting a clean record that includes sleep is worth more than extra minutes of noisy waking tracing.

procedures.title: Eye opening and eye closure
steps: Record a baseline with the patient relaxed, then instruct the patient to open and close the eyes on command and repeat several times through the study.
Keep each eyes-closed and eyes-open period long enough to see background reactivity (commonly several seconds to a minute; per your lab protocol).
Mark each eye opening and each eye closure on the record at the moment it happens.
Watch the patient during eye closure for fluttering or myoclonus of the eyelids, and note any clinical change during or just after closure.
Repeat eye opening and closure after drowsiness or sleep to check that the patient is again awake and reactive.
stop: Stop and notify the physician if a clinical event, loss of responsiveness or unusual eye movement or eyelid jerking appears with eye closure.
document: Mark each eye opening and closure on the record.
Note any change in the EEG or the patient's behavior on eye closure or eye opening.
procedures.tip: Clear, well-marked eye opening and closure lets the reader judge the posterior dominant rhythm's reactivity and recognize eye-closure-sensitive findings.

procedures.title: Hyperventilation
steps: Check the patient's history first and omit or modify the procedure for the conditions your protocol lists (for example recent stroke or intracranial hemorrhage, significant cardiopulmonary disease, sickle cell disease, moyamoya, or the patient being unable to cooperate).
Explain the procedure and obtain agreement, then record a baseline of a minute or so with eyes closed before starting.
Ask the patient to breathe deeply and steadily through the mouth, about 20 to 30 breaths per minute, with eyes closed and while seated or reclined and comfortable.
Continue for about 3 to 5 minutes (per your lab protocol, with most protocols requiring at least 3 minutes) and encourage good effort throughout, since effort determines adequacy.
Mark the start, the end and the effort quality, and note each minute elapsed.

Continue recording after the end of hyperventilation for at least 1 to 3 minutes (many labs use 3; per your lab protocol) with the patient breathing normally and quietly, with eyes closed then open, to watch the recovery.
Watch the patient's breathing, color and responsiveness throughout, and give a brief reassurance when needed.
stop: Stop immediately if a seizure begins, the patient is in distress, dizzy, faint or unable to continue, or a prolonged generalized discharge impairs responsiveness.
Call for help if a seizure or other event does not stop promptly or the patient does not recover to baseline.
During a brief burst, test responsiveness and follow your lab protocol on whether to continue; do not prolong hyperventilation once a seizure or prolonged discharge appears.
document: Mark start and end times, the quality of effort (good, fair, poor) and the patient's compliance.
Mark and describe any slowing, epileptiform discharge, clinical symptom or event during hyperventilation and during recovery.
Test and write down responsiveness during any generalized discharge or event, and record why the procedure was omitted or shortened if that occurred.
procedures.tip: Coach steady, deep, rhythmic breathing and keep the patient motivated, because poor effort is the most common reason hyperventilation fails to activate anything.

procedures.title: Intermittent photic stimulation
steps: Screen the history for known photosensitivity or seizures triggered by light and tell the physician before starting if there is any concern.
Place the strobe at about 30 cm from the patient's nasion, in a dimly lit room, and plan to run each frequency with eyes open and with eyes closed, per your lab protocol.
Deliver a series of flash trains over a range of frequencies (commonly from about 1 up to 30 Hz, with ascending and descending sequences; per your lab protocol).
Give each flash train for about 10 seconds with the eyes open, then with the eyes closed, with a short pause between trains.
Instruct the patient to keep the eyes open or closed as directed, and to not look away from the light during eyes-open trains.
Watch the record continuously as the frequency changes so that a response can be stopped immediately.
Use the same frequency sequence and stimulus settings as your lab protocol so studies remain comparable.
stop: Stop the flashing immediately when a generalized epileptiform discharge, a photoparoxysmal response or a seizure begins, or when the patient shows a clinical change, and then test responsiveness.
Call for help if a seizure occurs and follow your seizure-safety protocol.
Do not resume the sequence at that frequency until the physician says so or your lab protocol allows.
document: Mark the start and end of each flash train and write down the frequency, and whether eyes were open or closed.
Mark any photic driving, photoparoxysmal response, myoclonus, or clinical change and the frequency at which it occurred.
Note the time responsiveness was tested and the result, and any train omitted or stopped.
procedures.tip: A consistent, complete frequency series with clear marks lets the reader tie any response to the exact frequency and eye state.

procedures.title: Recording sleep
steps: Make the room dim and quiet, and let the patient lie back comfortably once the awake record and the other activations are complete, if the protocol allows.
Allow drowsiness and spontaneous sleep to develop and keep recording while the patient settles, with minimal talking or movement.
Watch the record for drowsiness and for the stages of non-REM sleep (vertex waves, spindles, K-complexes) and note the time of each change.
Avoid waking the patient when sleep is reached, but arouse the patient when your protocol or the clinical question requires a post-arousal record.
Record the arousal and the return to wakefulness, with a few minutes of the awake record after waking.
stop: Stop and call for help if the patient has an event during sleep, such as a seizure, abnormal movement, or apnea, and test responsiveness once they can be roused.
document: Mark the time of sleep onset, the stages reached and the arousal.
Describe any epileptiform activity during sleep as it appears, and any clinical event.
procedures.tip: A calm environment and a patient who is relaxed, not forced awake or rushed, gives the best chance of reaching true sleep within the recording time.

procedures.title: Sleep-deprived EEG
steps: Give the patient written instructions ahead of time about the amount of sleep to restrict (the exact amount, such as partial or total sleep restriction, depends on your lab protocol and the physician's order).

Tell the patient to avoid caffeine and sedating drinks as specified by the lab, to continue the usual medications unless the physician says otherwise, and to arrange safe transport since drowsiness is expected.
On arrival, confirm how much sleep the patient actually had and record it.
Keep the patient awake and out of bed until the recording begins, and record the standard waking portion and activations first.
Allow the patient to fall asleep in a dim, quiet room and keep recording through sleep and the awakening.
stop: Call for help or the physician if the patient is too drowsy to cooperate safely, or has a seizure or other event.
Do not ask a patient who is unsafe to drive to leave alone, and tell the physician or follow lab protocol.
document: Write down the sleep history, the hours of sleep restriction achieved and any stimulants or medications taken.
Mark sleep onset time and stages, any events, and the patient's condition at the end of the study.
procedures.tip: Confirm that the patient actually followed the sleep restriction instructions, since a patient who slept normally will not sleep-deprive and the study loses its purpose.

procedures.title: Video-EEG and monitoring
steps: Position the camera to capture the whole patient and the face, with adequate lighting, and confirm the video and EEG are time-synchronized.
Check the microphone and the push-button or marker so that both patient and observers can mark events.
Observe the patient continuously during the recording and instruct the patient, family or staff how to call for help and how to mark an event.
Keep the patient in view of the camera, and keep the bed, lighting and bedside rails safe and stable.
Review the video along with the EEG when marking an event so that the behavior and the tracing are matched.
stop: Go to the patient at once during any event that involves risk of injury, and call for help per your emergency protocol.
Stop the procedure if the patient is unsafe, and follow facility policy for safety and privacy.
document: Mark the time of every event and record whether it was marked by the patient, a family member, or the technologist.
Write down who was present, what was observed, and the patient's state before the event.
procedures.tip: Synchronized video with accurate, timely marks is what lets a reader decide whether an event had an EEG correlate.

procedures.title: Capturing and documenting clinical events
steps: Press the event marker as soon as a clinical event is seen or reported, and write the exact clock time.
Describe what you see as it happens, including the onset, the body parts involved, eye position, any vocalization, color, breathing and the duration.

Test responsiveness, awareness and memory at intervals during the event with a simple standardized routine: say the patient's name, ask them to repeat a word or phrase, give a command, and later ask them to recall it.
Test and record how the patient responds, including speech and motor function, and whether the patient can follow commands.
Stay with the patient, keep them safe, and keep recording through the recovery.
Ask the patient what they experienced afterward, and note whether they remember the test items given during the event.
stop: Call for help or the emergency team if a seizure lasts 5 minutes or longer (or per your facility's emergency protocol), seizures repeat without recovery, or there is a breathing problem, injury or any medical emergency.
Never restrain the patient or put anything in the mouth, and protect the head and keep the airway open.
document: Mark the start, the end, and the observed features of the event, the responsiveness testing and the results.
Note the time of recovery, the post-event state, and any injury or intervention by clinical staff.
procedures.tip: Early marking, a clear description and a consistent responsiveness check make a short event far more useful to the reading physician.

mistakes: Hyperventilation can be stopped as soon as the patient says they are tired.
Encourage steady effort for the full time set by your lab protocol (usually at least 3 minutes), and always record the recovery period afterward.
The recording ends when hyperventilation ends.
Keep recording for at least 1 to 3 minutes of recovery (per your lab protocol) because some changes appear or persist after the breathing stops.
Keep flashing through a generalized discharge to see how long it lasts.
Stop photic stimulation immediately when a generalized discharge, photoparoxysmal response or seizure begins, then test responsiveness and call for help if needed.
Photic stimulation can be done at one fixed frequency.
Use a range of frequencies (about 1 to 30 Hz in a set sequence per lab protocol) in both eyes-open and eyes-closed trains.
The technologist should say what the event is, such as an epileptic seizure.
Describe what you see and hear, mark it, and test responsiveness; the physician interprets the event and the diagnosis.
The strobe can be placed at any distance.
Place it at about 30 cm from the nasion (per your lab protocol) in a dim room so the stimulus is consistent.
A sleep-deprived study needs no confirmation of what the patient actually did.
Ask about and record the sleep actually obtained and any stimulants or medications taken.
Event marks and responsiveness testing can be added later from memory.
Mark the event at the moment it happens, write the clock time, and test and record responsiveness during the event.
